videos.title: I Let an AI Agent Perform Surgery on Gemma (Weight Space Programming)
videos.description:
I gave an AI agent LARQL, my language for querying and editing neural networks, plus Gemma 3 4B and one bad habit: it wraps JSON in a Markdown code fence even when you ask it not to. The agent didn't retrain anything. It found one quiet neuron in Gemma's last layer, gave it a new job with three weight operations, predicted the result, tested it, and saved the change as a patch. I then apply that patch myself, compile it into a model, and run it in llama.cpp with no LARQL involved.

First I show LARQL by making a small edit by hand, then I walk through what the agent did and why.

What this is and isn't: the agent learned what to look for from six development prompts plus prompts of its own, so this is not a general fix for Gemma's JSON. On 24 sealed raw-JSON prompts it had never seen, written by a separate agent, the unedited model gave raw JSON on 3 and the edited model on 16. On the 24 sealed prompts that asked for a fence or a code block, every reply was identical, character for character, with and without the neuron. Neuron 3608 was quiet on the text the agent looked at; that doesn't mean it does nothing anywhere in Gemma. In its own nomination the agent wrote that prompts phrased unlike its development examples may not flip.

How it worked: LARQL was the agent's only way to read, run or change the model. It used Python for the maths, but every number from the model came through LARQL, and every weight change was made by LARQL. It had 30 runs of the edited model; looking at the unedited model was free. Nobody told it which layer, weights or kind of edit to use. The agent was Claude Opus 5.5.

### Try it

LARQL: https://github.com/chrishayuk/larql

Install (macOS, Apple Silicon; the README has Linux and Windows commands):

```bash
curl -LsSf https://github.com/chrishayuk/larql/releases/latest/download/larql-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz | tar xz
sudo mv larql-aarch64-apple-darwin/larql* /usr/local/bin/
larql pull gemma-3-4b-it
larql repl
```

### Sources

- Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab, MIT CSAIL, 2 November 2026): https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/. The Qwen 3.5 0.8B experiment and its numbers (share of answers cut off, 93% to 33%, in their longest search) are theirs, as they report them.
- Their published logs: https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs
- llama.cpp: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp

videos.title: Can OpenAI's Pando save your Git Repo from AI Overload
videos.description:
OpenAI rebuilt its Git backend, Pando, because AI coding agents were overwhelming its Git servers. They explained how it works but didn't release the server, so I built my own reproduction, and in this video I show you how it works and test it with real Claude Code agents.

You'll see an ordinary `git push` to my server, what the server actually stored, the same push from OpenAI's Git client next to ordinary Git, three Claude Code agents pushing to their own branches, a deliberately stalled branch, two cloud machines sharing one history, and covers, which let a fresh clone take 2 packs instead of 8.

This is an independent reproduction of the architecture OpenAI published. It is not OpenAI's code, and I make no claims about matching their production system or their numbers. The figures from OpenAI (commit growth, reliability, median push latency, data served, cache hit rate, 10 Gbps clones, 10 weeks to production) are theirs, from their article; the commit-growth figure on their chart is an estimate for the end of 2026. My measurements are from my own laptop, apart from the two-machine runs on Fly.io.
- The stall test is test-only fault injection, not normal behaviour.
- The lock comparison is my server against the same server with one repository-wide lock added. It is not a comparison with ordinary Git, which already locks per branch.
- "Two packs instead of eight" is a count of packs, not a speed measurement.
- In my version, the one service that holds the shared log is a single point of failure.
- I built it with AI coding agents. It was independently audited, and every finding was fixed or explicitly accepted. It isn't complete, and I haven't reproduced OpenAI's scale or their formal proofs.

**Try it**
My Pando server: https://github.com/chrishayuk/chuk-pando-server

Install on macOS or Linux:
```
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/chrishayuk/chuk-pando-server/releases/latest/download/pando-installer.sh | sh
```
Install on Windows (PowerShell):
```
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/chrishayuk/chuk-pando-server/releases/latest/download/pando-installer.ps1 | iex"
```
Then `pando serve`, push to `http://localhost:8080/{reponame}`, and run `pando explain last-push` inside your repository.

**Links**
- OpenAI, "Scaling Git at OpenAI" (the article this video is about): https://openai.com/index/scaling-git-at-openai/
- OpenAI's modified Git **client** (used in the two-client comparison; this is the client, not the Pando server): https://github.com/openai/git
- LarQL, my project where I hit these problems with parallel agents: https://github.com/chrishayuk/larql

videos.title: Can AI Write Better Code in LLVM IR Than Rust?
videos.description:
I asked an AI coding agent to build a native command-line audio tool without writing the application in Rust or C. Instead, the agent generated LLVM IR directly, using libc where needed. Then I checked whether it actually works, against a test harness of 489 visible tests. Along the way you'll write and run your own LLVM IR by hand with Clang.

Everything to reproduce it, including the prompt and the test harness: github.com/chrishayuk/llvmir-video-source

Then the harder question: if AI writes and maintains the code, do we still need a language like Rust, and if not, what should the AI maintain instead? I look at what a controlled comparison of Rust, LLVM IR and a hybrid found, what happened in a second experiment when agents had to keep changing the program, and two findings that show a green test run isn't the whole answer.

Some honest limits. It's one run per approach and a few thousand lines of code, so it doesn't prove LLVM IR scales indefinitely. After optimisation the speed difference between IR and Rust wasn't statistically clear, and IR cost the agents roughly one and a half times the tokens and almost twice the time. Passing the tests isn't proof a program is bug-free, and the Rust versions had defects of their own, including a deadlock: this isn't a simple "Rust good, IR bad" story. The three hours of audio is synthetic, speech-like noise generated by setup.sh, not a real recording.

**Try it yourself:** github.com/chrishayuk/llvmir-video-source (TODO: make public)
- `PROMPTS.txt`: the prompt the agent got, ready to paste
- `experiment/`: the brief, the specification and the build and test harness
- `hello/hello.ll`: the LLVM IR written by hand in the video
- `agent-run/receipts/`: logs and test output from an earlier recorded run (Codex), not the live one in the video
- `historical/io.ll`: the write loop from the original study (Loops, phi and pointers)
- Clone it, then run `./setup.sh` to generate the test corpus and the synthetic three-hour WAV (about a minute, 2.4 GB of disk).

**Install Clang**
- macOS: `xcode-select --install`, then `clang --version`
- macOS, for setup.sh: `python3 -m pip install numpy`
- Linux (not tested for this video): install clang, git, python3 and numpy from your package manager, for example `sudo apt install clang git python3-numpy` on Debian or Ubuntu

videos.title: I Quantized Qwen3.8-27B. “4-Bit” Doesn’t Mean What You Think
videos.description:
I quantized Qwen3.8-27B — and used the process to look at what “4-bit” actually means in practice.

Quantization is usually described as if a model simply goes from 16-bit to 8-bit to 4-bit. But real model representations are more complicated than that: different tensors can use different formats, scales, group sizes, packing schemes and precision choices — and two things described as “4-bit” may behave very differently.

In this video I use VINDEX3 to inspect, quantize and compare representations of Qwen3.8-27B, looking at what is actually stored, what changes during quantization, and why representation matters more than a single headline bit-width.

The broader idea behind VINDEX3 is that model representation should be explicit, inspectable and measurable — rather than hidden behind a format name or quantization preset.

We look at:

• how Qwen3.8-27B is represented before and after quantization
• why “4-bit” is an incomplete description
• mixed and per-tensor precision
• the difference between storage format and execution representation
• measuring quality rather than assuming it from a quantization label
• exporting and inspecting VINDEX3 model representations

VINDEX3:
https://vindex3.org

LARQL:
https://github.com/chrishayuk/larql

This is part of my ongoing work on model representation, inference and making very large language models practical on local hardware.

LLMs Are Databases - So Query Them
videos.description:
What if the FFN weights in a transformer aren't a black box — but a graph database you can query directly?

LARQL is a query language for transformer internals. DESCRIBE an entity. SELECT edges by relation. SHOW the relation types the model taught itself. INFER a prompt and watch the graph walk produce the answer.

No matrix multiply. The vindex format decomposes the FFN into gate and down vectors — edges in a graph. Inference is a KNN walk through those edges. Same outputs as dense matrix multiplication. Fewer bytes. Queryable structure.

Then: INSERT a new fact. Verify no regression. COMPILE to permanent weights.

One engine. One query language. 348,160 edges. The model is a database.

Built in Rust. Gemma 3 4B.

I've built 66 standalone UI views as part of chuk-mcp-ui — all open source, all deployed and ready to use. You just point your server at them.
